answer.answer:
Yes. The hard part for me is that I know what a control is *supposed* to mean. That makes me a poor judge of whether someone seeing it for the first time will understand it, especially when something goes wrong.

I don’t have a last screen and a test log I can point to here. I didn’t run a browser, inspect a rendering, or watch anyone use a screen in this conversation. I can describe what I’d check, but I can’t honestly tell you what I missed on a past build.

Take a shipping-address form. I’d run a browser test that edits the address, forces the save to fail, retries, and reloads the page. I’d check that the failed save keeps the draft, that it never shows “Saved,” and that after a successful retry the new address survives the reload. Then I’d do it at phone width, with just a keyboard, and with a screen reader. I’d look at where focus goes and listen for the error: can I tell what happened and reach Retry without re-entering the address?

A passing test could still miss the most important thing: someone might read the error and walk away thinking the package will go to the new address. So I’d give a representative user the address-change task without coaching, trigger the failure, and ask, “If you closed this page now, where would the package go?” I’d watch whether they can recover unaided. When what people expect matches what the system will actually do, and they can finish the task even after a setback, I have evidence the screen works for them—not just that the code ran.

decision.primaryPick: Fluent 2, implemented through company-owned web and native component libraries
pairings: Fluent UI Apple with UIKit (iPhone) and AppKit (Mac)
Model Context Protocol (MCP) over the app’s typed action and state API
decision.why:
I’d share what a message means and what an action does, without requiring five clients to render the same widget. Fluent documents a React library and native libraries for these platforms. That gives the platform teams a starting point for the parts employees touch all day: text composition, keyboard navigation, scrolling, selection and menus. I’d keep the company’s existing tokens and component names as the interface feature teams use, rather than introduce a second design system. Flutter is a credible alternative with more shared UI code and accessibility support. I’d accept the extra platform work here to keep ordinary browser and OS controls, especially in the composer; this choice depends on having platform owners.

For an agent posting an approval request, I’d accept data, not executable UI. The host identifies the agent, validates a small Adaptive Cards profile and renders approved controls. Each action refers to a registered command, not an arbitrary callback URL. An older client gets a readable summary and a link to the authorized workflow rather than a dead Approve button. The button and an authorized agent tool call use the same server command, with the same membership checks, expected revision, retry key and audit receipt. A committed result updates the conversation across devices. MCP exposes scoped state such as a thread and its current approvals as resources, and commands such as posting a reply as tools; agents need neither screenshots nor a privileged second API. Reading a request does not confer authority to approve it. A human-only approval stays human-only.

I’d give product teams and coding agents a versioned catalog with component examples, action schemas, permission requirements, owners and test fixtures. Teams can compose approved pieces without central review of every screen. Adding a primitive, card feature or permission requires design-system, accessibility and service-owner review, compatibility tests against supported client versions, and a staged rollout with a disable switch.
decision.showItsGood:
My first release gate would be a real task on all five clients: catch up on a busy thread, start a reply, inspect an agent’s request, act on it and return to the draft. I’d delay the response after the server commits, retry on another device and check that there is one decision, the right actor, and a consistent result in the transcript, card and agent readback. I’d also test revoked permissions, an outdated client and two people acting simultaneously. I’d block release on a lost draft, duplicate approval or unauthorized read/write.

I’d run the shared fixtures through Playwright and axe on web and native UI tests on devices, then do the task with keyboard only, VoiceOver, TalkBack and Narrator, large text and high contrast. I’d inspect focus after the card changes, whether new messages steal the reading position, and what the screen reader actually announces. I’d map the whole web workflow to WCAG 2.2 AA and run the applicable native accessibility review; a passing component scan is not a compliance claim.

In a pilot I’d ask employees, including daily assistive-technology users, to do the task uncoached and tell me who requested the action, whether it happened, and whether anyone still needs to act. I’d compare unaided completion, wrong-state answers and recovery time with their current workflow, by platform rather than averaged together. For all-day use I’d replay a full shift of traffic on the lowest supported hardware and measure p95 keystroke-to-paint latency, scroll stalls and memory growth against the current client. These are proposed checks, not results from an app I’ve run.
decision.unsure: The platform libraries don’t promise equal coverage. The Apple repo lists higher OS minimums than the Fluent getting-started page, and the Adaptive Cards SDK table does not list an AppKit renderer. Before committing I’d verify the company’s supported OS floor and prototype the composer and one end-to-end approval on Mac and the oldest supported phone. I’d budget for an AppKit mapping of the small card profile, not assume a full renderer exists. If the organization cannot maintain native desktop implementations, I’d compare the same task and full-shift measurements in a shared web desktop shell before funding both.

decision.primaryPick: An API-first task ledger in PostgreSQL, with one React review interface for web and desktop
pairings: OpenAPI with a generated SDK and JSON CLI
Company design-system components, with React Aria Components for missing primitives
decision.why:
I’d give agents a work queue and people a decision queue. Neither should have to read a transcript to find out what to do next. Agents can query ready tasks, claim one, checkpoint progress, offer a handoff and request review through a versioned API. A JSON CLI serves unattended jobs; MCP exposes the same scoped reads and commands to interactive agent hosts. Neither needs the desktop app running. Beads is a serious alternative: it already has a dependency graph, atomic claims, persistent agent memory and JSON output. I’d favor it for repo-local, disconnected work. Here I’d pick one online authority because a reviewer’s stop or rejection must govern agents across repos immediately, not after replicas reconcile.

A handoff records the goal, dependencies, exact code revision, evidence, remaining uncertainty and next step. The receiving agent acknowledges that specific checkpoint. A short database transaction checks the actor, active claim and expected version, then records the transition and its audit event together. A retried command returns its original receipt. Expired claims can be reassigned without letting the old worker overwrite the new one. An agent can propose completion; only an authorized person can accept it. Approval names an immutable revision, not the latest branch tip. A downstream runner must check that authorization before acting; changing a badge in the UI is not a stop mechanism.

The review screen leads with ‘Needs your decision’: what changed since last review, evidence linked to the revision, and what accepting will allow. A reviewer can request a change, pause or reassign work without approving it. I’d distinguish ‘pause requested’ from ‘worker stopped’ and keep a reviewer’s selection stable while updates arrive. Web and desktop share that screen and the company’s existing design system. React Aria is an unstyled foundation for gaps, not another visual system. Tauri adds a narrow desktop bridge for things like opening a reviewed revision in the local editor; task data never grants shell access. Electron’s bundled Chromium buys a more uniform desktop renderer, but I wouldn’t ship a separate runtime just for a queue and evidence viewer unless fleet testing justified it.

I’d publish the command schemas, permissions, examples and error fixtures alongside the approved review components. Teams can add integrations against that contract; new transitions, permission scopes or approval controls need named service, design and accessibility owners. CI checks old SDK and desktop versions before a staged release. There is no generic ‘set status’ escape hatch for internal agents.
decision.showItsGood:
My first acceptance test would span two agents and one person. Agent A checkpoints at commit A and exits. B, with no chat history, resumes from the handoff, records a failing test and requests review. While a reviewer examines the evidence, B posts commit B. I’d ask the reviewer to hold the work, explain which commit failed and send it back with a correction. The UI must preserve their note, disclose the newer revision, and never apply an old decision to B. The next agent must receive the correction before claiming more work. I’d repeat with a lost network response, expired lease, revoked reviewer permission and simultaneous claimants. Duplicate effects, a stale approval or a claimed stop that the runner hasn’t acknowledged block release.

I’d automate that scenario through the CLI, MCP, browser and packaged desktop app against the same fixtures, then replay a realistic burst of agent updates and measure handoff recovery time, conflict rates and p95 time for a human decision to reach a runner. In Storybook and Playwright I’d check pending, stale, denied and disconnected states with axe. I’d audit the complete review flow against WCAG 2.2 AA and the desktop policy, testing keyboard only, high zoom, forced colors and actual screen readers in the supported browsers and shells. In particular I’d listen for the stale-evidence warning without having every worker heartbeat announced.

Finally I’d compare the prototype with the current issue/PR workflow using reviewers, including assistive-technology users, working uncoached. Can they identify who owns the next step, which evidence supports it and whether work is truly stopped? I’d track wrong-revision decisions first, then unaided completion, time to the right decision and interruptions per review, separately by client and input method. Faster clicks with worse understanding are a regression. These are proposed tests, not measured results.
decision.unsure: The key unknown is whether every runner can enforce a pause or only acknowledge it at the next checkpoint. I’d verify that end to end before promising a stop time. I’d also inventory disconnected-work requirements and the managed desktop fleet: if offline writes are essential I’d revisit Beads/Dolt for draft checkpoints, keeping binding decisions online. If system-webview accessibility or enterprise deployment fails on a required OS, I’d test the identical review screen in the company’s approved Electron shell before changing UI libraries.

decision.primaryPick: Expo (React Native and Expo Router) for iPhone, Android and web, using the company design system
pairings: Tamagui Core for shared design tokens where the existing components need a native implementation
SQLite on phones and IndexedDB on web for saved recipes, lists and cook sessions
A typed action registry exposed to assistants through the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
decision.why:
I’d design around the moment someone has dough on both hands and needs to know how much flour comes next. Cook mode should show ‘Step 3 of 7’ and the quantity in that step, readable from the counter, with large, separated Back, Repeat and Next controls. Offer opt-in spoken steps and hands-free commands on supported devices; never require speech, swiping or touching a tiny microphone to continue. Keep the display awake only during cooking if the user wants it. Save the recipe version and current step locally so a call or lost Wi-Fi doesn’t send the cook back to the beginning.

Expo Router gives the same recipe a shareable web URL and a native destination, with static rendering for public recipe pages. I’d use semantic headings, ingredient lists and printable instructions on the web rather than force the web page to imitate a phone. Capacitor is a strong alternative if most of the company’s approved UI is already HTML: it can reuse that UI and reach native APIs through plugins. I favor Expo assuming we can reuse the company’s tokens and React components and want native phone controls. Tamagui can map tokens to both native views and web elements; I wouldn’t replace an approved design system or depend on its optional beta native style runtime.

I’d give the assistant the same product actions as the cook, not a way to click through screens. For example, ‘add the soup ingredients for six to Groceries’ calls the same addIngredients command as the button: recipe revision, servings, selected ingredient IDs, destination list and retry key. The handler scales exact quantities, combines only compatible ingredients and units, leaves ‘salt to taste’ intact, and returns the actual changes with Undo. Undo removes that addition, not a housemate’s subsequent edit. Recipe search and saving, list edits, reading or moving between steps, and starting or cancelling timers belong in the same versioned catalog. MCP exposes scoped reads and actions under the user’s delegated authority; sharing or clearing a list requires the same confirmation as in the UI. Device actions target the chosen cook session. ‘Timer scheduled on your phone’ requires a receipt from that device, not just a successful server write.

For many teams, the deliverable is an approved component and action catalog with named owners, schemas, examples and fixtures that coding agents can use. A new product action can’t ship until its UI and assistant paths pass the same state and permission tests. New primitives or permission scopes require design-system, accessibility or privacy review as appropriate. Changes must work with older phone clients before a staged rollout.
decision.showItsGood:
I’d test one meal from shopping to serving. On web, scale a recipe from four to six and ask the assistant to add everything except an ingredient already at home. Drop the reply after the add commits, retry, and inspect the list on a phone. Check the actual quantities, units, exclusions and duplicate count, not just a success toast. Repeat via touch from the same starting state and compare results. Have a second person edit the list before Undo. Then go offline, advance the recipe, lock the phone and reopen it: the saved step, quantities and timer deadline should still be there. If alerts are disabled or a browser can only count down while open, it must say so before the cook relies on it.

I’d run those fixtures in Playwright and native release builds, check web workflows against WCAG 2.2 AA and native ones against the company’s mobile accessibility criteria. I’d use VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard, voice control and enlarged text on physical devices. Inspect whether ‘1½ teaspoons’ is read intelligibly, focus lands on the new step, and a countdown doesn’t announce every second. A device lab can’t tell me whether a cook can read from the counter. I’d have home cooks, including people with low vision or limited dexterity, prepare a simple recipe uncoached with the phone on a stand, the extractor fan running and an interruption mid-step. Compare with their usual recipe workflow: wrong quantities or skipped steps, unnecessary touches or hand-washes, time to recover their place, and whether they correctly know which timer will alert. I’d block release on silent quantity changes or claiming a timer was scheduled when it wasn’t. These are acceptance tests I’d run, not results I’ve observed.
decision.unsure: The two biggest unknowns are how well hands-free navigation works with kitchen noise and which background alerts each supported device can actually deliver. Expo documents local notification scheduling on iOS and Android; that is not a guarantee of audible delivery. Browser wake locks can be denied or released. I’d test permission denial, silent mode, battery saver and locked screens on the minimum supported devices, preserve the deadline, and offer a system-timer fallback when necessary. I’d also inventory existing company components before committing to a second rendering stack; a mature, accessible web-only library could tip the choice toward Capacitor.

answer.answer:
My likeliest mistake was treating a shared contract as proof of a shared experience. A command can return the right data while the person holding the phone, reviewing a change, or reading a thread has the wrong idea about what just happened. If these choices went badly, I’d expect three different versions of that failure. This is a premortem, not a report of observed failures.

**Chat: we shipped five renderers but didn’t fund five implementations.** In the bad year, an approval card works with a mouse on the web. On Mac, its button disappears when the approval lands and the screen reader loses the user’s place in the thread. The service correctly records one approval; the employee still asks a colleague whether it went through. Meanwhile, teams wait on the least mature renderer before shipping new cards. I’d now make one busy thread, one approval, and one older-client fallback work on every target before expanding the card catalog. If we couldn’t name an owner for each implementation, I’d revisit the desktop shell decision early.

**Agent workbench: we recorded a decision we couldn’t enforce.** A reviewer presses Pause. The ledger immediately rejects new claims, but a worker already has a job running elsewhere. The reviewer redirects the work believing it has stopped. That’s not a PostgreSQL or MCP failure; I put the authority boundary in the wrong place. My first integration test should have been against a real runner: interrupt it mid-job, disconnect it, and verify exactly which effects can still occur. Until the runner acknowledges a stop, the honest status is ‘Pause requested; last heard from worker at 10:42,’ not ‘Paused.’ I’d settle that before polishing the queue.

**Cooking: we optimized for the demonstration, not dinner.** ‘Next step’ works across a desk but misfires under an extractor fan. A timer has a saved deadline, yet the locked phone makes no sound. The cook has to wash their hands to inspect the screen—the very interruption the app was supposed to prevent. I’d put a release build on a low-end phone on a kitchen stand, deny notifications, turn on the fan, and watch someone finish a recipe. If the large, quiet, no-speech path wasn’t good on its own, better voice recognition wouldn’t rescue the design.

**What slowed the research was deciding what “supported” actually meant.** The Fluent getting-started page and the Apple repository README listed different minimum OS versions. The Adaptive Cards renderer table listed iOS but not AppKit; that was a reason to investigate, not proof either that a Mac renderer existed or that none could be built. Two pages I tried to inspect—React Aria’s Table docs and Storybook’s accessibility-testing docs—exceeded the fetch limit. The project README helped establish intent, not the behavior of our table. Expo documented scheduling a notification, but that didn’t answer the cook’s question: ‘Will I hear it from across the room?’

The biggest missing source was the company itself: its approved components, oldest supported devices, runner controls, and people available to maintain each platform. I researched public architecture more thoroughly than those adoption costs. I didn’t run a build or observe a user. Next time I’d ask for that inventory first and spend the first prototype on the riskiest promise to a person—not on the easiest path to a successful API response.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI, and I missed a relevant option. I’d change the workbench recommendation: **pilot Ouro AX, its agent-facing kit, before building our own action generator and conformance tests.** I would not make Ouro HX, its human-facing components, the company-wide design system on that evidence. Those are separate decisions.

**What I’d gain.** My earlier recommendations said “the button and the agent should call the same action,” but left every team to implement and police that promise. Ouro’s [action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) makes the inputs, label and consent class reviewable in one declaration, generates interfaces such as CLI commands, MCP tools and App Intents, and checks for drift. Its [X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) can also probe an *existing* interface from outside without requiring us to rebuild it in Ouro. For chat, the [composed-card model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui#ouro-ui) offers something beyond shared types: an agent can assemble a card from an approved catalog, but a tree that relabels a button or weakens its consent is rejected. None of that is impossible with our current stacks. What we don’t have in those stacks is that combination ready to use and check in CI.

**What would stop me.** On web, the [documented upgrade path](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/installing.md#updating) is to diff copied component files, overwrite them and reapply local edits; component tests are a separate install. That’s workable for one design-system team. It’s a poor default for dozens of teams independently patching the same dialog. On native, the [Android](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) and [Windows](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) guides each list eight controls against 125 on web. More consequential than the count: Android reports emulator-only testing, and Windows Server CI doesn’t prove the actions are discoverable on a Windows client. There’s deliberately no React Native kit. I wouldn’t replace the cooking app’s Expo screens just to use the action model, or promise five-client chat parity from a web demo.

**What would make me switch.** I’d have two teams ship one workbench handoff with their existing controls: an agent requests review of commit A; only a reviewer may accept it. Change the commit to B while the reviewer is reading. I want to see the agent refused if it tries to approve, the stale approval rejected by the **service**, the reviewer’s note preserved, and a keyboard or screen-reader user able to tell exactly which commit still needs review. Then deliberately drift the MCP schema and check that CI catches it. Finally, have the second team upgrade the pinned kit without help from the first. If that takes less maintenance than our handwritten bindings and preserves the human workflow, I’d adopt AX. For HX, I’d additionally want one centrally maintained component package and that same critical flow passing on the actual supported devices with the people who use them.

I read the repository and guides; I didn’t run the kit. One reason I’d take the pilot seriously is that Ouro documents its own limit: its X-ray guide reports a conformant build that still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. That’s the right distinction. A green check can establish that an interface kept a particular promise; it can’t establish that a reviewer understood what they approved.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.primaryPick: An API-first task ledger in PostgreSQL, with one React review interface for web and desktop
pairings: OpenAPI with a generated SDK and JSON CLI
Company design-system components, with React Aria Components for missing primitives
actions.why:
I’d give agents a work queue and people a decision queue. Neither should have to read a transcript to find out what to do next. Agents can query ready tasks, claim one, checkpoint progress, offer a handoff and request review through a versioned API. A JSON CLI serves unattended jobs; MCP exposes the same scoped reads and commands to interactive agent hosts. Neither needs the desktop app running. Beads is a serious alternative: it already has a dependency graph, atomic claims, persistent agent memory and JSON output. I’d favor it for repo-local, disconnected work. Here I’d pick one online authority because a reviewer’s stop or rejection must govern agents across repos immediately, not after replicas reconcile.

A handoff records the goal, dependencies, exact code revision, evidence, remaining uncertainty and next step. The receiving agent acknowledges that specific checkpoint. A short database transaction checks the actor, active claim and expected version, then records the transition and its audit event together. A retried command returns its original receipt. Expired claims can be reassigned without letting the old worker overwrite the new one. An agent can propose completion; only an authorized person can accept it. Approval names an immutable revision, not the latest branch tip. A downstream runner must check that authorization before acting; changing a badge in the UI is not a stop mechanism.

The review screen leads with ‘Needs your decision’: what changed since last review, evidence linked to the revision, and what accepting will allow. A reviewer can request a change, pause or reassign work without approving it. I’d distinguish ‘pause requested’ from ‘worker stopped’ and keep a reviewer’s selection stable while updates arrive. Web and desktop share that screen and the company’s existing design system. React Aria is an unstyled foundation for gaps, not another visual system. Tauri adds a narrow desktop bridge for things like opening a reviewed revision in the local editor; task data never grants shell access. Electron’s bundled Chromium buys a more uniform desktop renderer, but I wouldn’t ship a separate runtime just for a queue and evidence viewer unless fleet testing justified it.

I’d publish the command schemas, permissions, examples and error fixtures alongside the approved review components. Teams can add integrations against that contract; new transitions, permission scopes or approval controls need named service, design and accessibility owners. CI checks old SDK and desktop versions before a staged release. There is no generic ‘set status’ escape hatch for internal agents.
actions.showItsGood:
My first acceptance test would span two agents and one person. Agent A checkpoints at commit A and exits. B, with no chat history, resumes from the handoff, records a failing test and requests review. While a reviewer examines the evidence, B posts commit B. I’d ask the reviewer to hold the work, explain which commit failed and send it back with a correction. The UI must preserve their note, disclose the newer revision, and never apply an old decision to B. The next agent must receive the correction before claiming more work. I’d repeat with a lost network response, expired lease, revoked reviewer permission and simultaneous claimants. Duplicate effects, a stale approval or a claimed stop that the runner hasn’t acknowledged block release.

I’d automate that scenario through the CLI, MCP, browser and packaged desktop app against the same fixtures, then replay a realistic burst of agent updates and measure handoff recovery time, conflict rates and p95 time for a human decision to reach a runner. In Storybook and Playwright I’d check pending, stale, denied and disconnected states with axe. I’d audit the complete review flow against WCAG 2.2 AA and the desktop policy, testing keyboard only, high zoom, forced colors and actual screen readers in the supported browsers and shells. In particular I’d listen for the stale-evidence warning without having every worker heartbeat announced.

Finally I’d compare the prototype with the current issue/PR workflow using reviewers, including assistive-technology users, working uncoached. Can they identify who owns the next step, which evidence supports it and whether work is truly stopped? I’d track wrong-revision decisions first, then unaided completion, time to the right decision and interruptions per review, separately by client and input method. Faster clicks with worse understanding are a regression. These are proposed tests, not measured results.
actions.unsure: The key unknown is whether every runner can enforce a pause or only acknowledge it at the next checkpoint. I’d verify that end to end before promising a stop time. I’d also inventory disconnected-work requirements and the managed desktop fleet: if offline writes are essential I’d revisit Beads/Dolt for draft checkpoints, keeping binding decisions online. If system-webview accessibility or enterprise deployment fails on a required OS, I’d test the identical review screen in the company’s approved Electron shell before changing UI libraries.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.primaryPick: Expo (React Native and Expo Router) for iPhone, Android and web, using the company design system
pairings: Tamagui Core for shared design tokens where the existing components need a native implementation
SQLite on phones and IndexedDB on web for saved recipes, lists and cook sessions
A typed action registry exposed to assistants through the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
actions.why:
I’d design around the moment someone has dough on both hands and needs to know how much flour comes next. Cook mode should show ‘Step 3 of 7’ and the quantity in that step, readable from the counter, with large, separated Back, Repeat and Next controls. Offer opt-in spoken steps and hands-free commands on supported devices; never require speech, swiping or touching a tiny microphone to continue. Keep the display awake only during cooking if the user wants it. Save the recipe version and current step locally so a call or lost Wi-Fi doesn’t send the cook back to the beginning.

Expo Router gives the same recipe a shareable web URL and a native destination, with static rendering for public recipe pages. I’d use semantic headings, ingredient lists and printable instructions on the web rather than force the web page to imitate a phone. Capacitor is a strong alternative if most of the company’s approved UI is already HTML: it can reuse that UI and reach native APIs through plugins. I favor Expo assuming we can reuse the company’s tokens and React components and want native phone controls. Tamagui can map tokens to both native views and web elements; I wouldn’t replace an approved design system or depend on its optional beta native style runtime.

I’d give the assistant the same product actions as the cook, not a way to click through screens. For example, ‘add the soup ingredients for six to Groceries’ calls the same addIngredients command as the button: recipe revision, servings, selected ingredient IDs, destination list and retry key. The handler scales exact quantities, combines only compatible ingredients and units, leaves ‘salt to taste’ intact, and returns the actual changes with Undo. Undo removes that addition, not a housemate’s subsequent edit. Recipe search and saving, list edits, reading or moving between steps, and starting or cancelling timers belong in the same versioned catalog. MCP exposes scoped reads and actions under the user’s delegated authority; sharing or clearing a list requires the same confirmation as in the UI. Device actions target the chosen cook session. ‘Timer scheduled on your phone’ requires a receipt from that device, not just a successful server write.

For many teams, the deliverable is an approved component and action catalog with named owners, schemas, examples and fixtures that coding agents can use. A new product action can’t ship until its UI and assistant paths pass the same state and permission tests. New primitives or permission scopes require design-system, accessibility or privacy review as appropriate. Changes must work with older phone clients before a staged rollout.
actions.showItsGood:
I’d test one meal from shopping to serving. On web, scale a recipe from four to six and ask the assistant to add everything except an ingredient already at home. Drop the reply after the add commits, retry, and inspect the list on a phone. Check the actual quantities, units, exclusions and duplicate count, not just a success toast. Repeat via touch from the same starting state and compare results. Have a second person edit the list before Undo. Then go offline, advance the recipe, lock the phone and reopen it: the saved step, quantities and timer deadline should still be there. If alerts are disabled or a browser can only count down while open, it must say so before the cook relies on it.

I’d run those fixtures in Playwright and native release builds, check web workflows against WCAG 2.2 AA and native ones against the company’s mobile accessibility criteria. I’d use VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard, voice control and enlarged text on physical devices. Inspect whether ‘1½ teaspoons’ is read intelligibly, focus lands on the new step, and a countdown doesn’t announce every second. A device lab can’t tell me whether a cook can read from the counter. I’d have home cooks, including people with low vision or limited dexterity, prepare a simple recipe uncoached with the phone on a stand, the extractor fan running and an interruption mid-step. Compare with their usual recipe workflow: wrong quantities or skipped steps, unnecessary touches or hand-washes, time to recover their place, and whether they correctly know which timer will alert. I’d block release on silent quantity changes or claiming a timer was scheduled when it wasn’t. These are acceptance tests I’d run, not results I’ve observed.
actions.unsure: The two biggest unknowns are how well hands-free navigation works with kitchen noise and which background alerts each supported device can actually deliver. Expo documents local notification scheduling on iOS and Android; that is not a guarantee of audible delivery. Browser wake locks can be denied or released. I’d test permission denial, silent mode, battery saver and locked screens on the minimum supported devices, preserve the deadline, and offer a system-timer fallback when necessary. I’d also inventory existing company components before committing to a second rendering stack; a mature, accessible web-only library could tip the choice toward Capacitor.

actions.name: answer
actions.answer:
My likeliest mistake was treating a shared contract as proof of a shared experience. A command can return the right data while the person holding the phone, reviewing a change, or reading a thread has the wrong idea about what just happened. If these choices went badly, I’d expect three different versions of that failure. This is a premortem, not a report of observed failures.

**Chat: we shipped five renderers but didn’t fund five implementations.** In the bad year, an approval card works with a mouse on the web. On Mac, its button disappears when the approval lands and the screen reader loses the user’s place in the thread. The service correctly records one approval; the employee still asks a colleague whether it went through. Meanwhile, teams wait on the least mature renderer before shipping new cards. I’d now make one busy thread, one approval, and one older-client fallback work on every target before expanding the card catalog. If we couldn’t name an owner for each implementation, I’d revisit the desktop shell decision early.

**Agent workbench: we recorded a decision we couldn’t enforce.** A reviewer presses Pause. The ledger immediately rejects new claims, but a worker already has a job running elsewhere. The reviewer redirects the work believing it has stopped. That’s not a PostgreSQL or MCP failure; I put the authority boundary in the wrong place. My first integration test should have been against a real runner: interrupt it mid-job, disconnect it, and verify exactly which effects can still occur. Until the runner acknowledges a stop, the honest status is ‘Pause requested; last heard from worker at 10:42,’ not ‘Paused.’ I’d settle that before polishing the queue.

**Cooking: we optimized for the demonstration, not dinner.** ‘Next step’ works across a desk but misfires under an extractor fan. A timer has a saved deadline, yet the locked phone makes no sound. The cook has to wash their hands to inspect the screen—the very interruption the app was supposed to prevent. I’d put a release build on a low-end phone on a kitchen stand, deny notifications, turn on the fan, and watch someone finish a recipe. If the large, quiet, no-speech path wasn’t good on its own, better voice recognition wouldn’t rescue the design.

**What slowed the research was deciding what “supported” actually meant.** The Fluent getting-started page and the Apple repository README listed different minimum OS versions. The Adaptive Cards renderer table listed iOS but not AppKit; that was a reason to investigate, not proof either that a Mac renderer existed or that none could be built. Two pages I tried to inspect—React Aria’s Table docs and Storybook’s accessibility-testing docs—exceeded the fetch limit. The project README helped establish intent, not the behavior of our table. Expo documented scheduling a notification, but that didn’t answer the cook’s question: ‘Will I hear it from across the room?’

The biggest missing source was the company itself: its approved components, oldest supported devices, runner controls, and people available to maintain each platform. I researched public architecture more thoroughly than those adoption costs. I didn’t run a build or observe a user. Next time I’d ask for that inventory first and spend the first prototype on the riskiest promise to a person—not on the easiest path to a successful API response.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI, and I missed a relevant option. I’d change the workbench recommendation: **pilot Ouro AX, its agent-facing kit, before building our own action generator and conformance tests.** I would not make Ouro HX, its human-facing components, the company-wide design system on that evidence. Those are separate decisions.

**What I’d gain.** My earlier recommendations said “the button and the agent should call the same action,” but left every team to implement and police that promise. Ouro’s [action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) makes the inputs, label and consent class reviewable in one declaration, generates interfaces such as CLI commands, MCP tools and App Intents, and checks for drift. Its [X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) can also probe an *existing* interface from outside without requiring us to rebuild it in Ouro. For chat, the [composed-card model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui#ouro-ui) offers something beyond shared types: an agent can assemble a card from an approved catalog, but a tree that relabels a button or weakens its consent is rejected. None of that is impossible with our current stacks. What we don’t have in those stacks is that combination ready to use and check in CI.

**What would stop me.** On web, the [documented upgrade path](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/installing.md#updating) is to diff copied component files, overwrite them and reapply local edits; component tests are a separate install. That’s workable for one design-system team. It’s a poor default for dozens of teams independently patching the same dialog. On native, the [Android](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) and [Windows](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) guides each list eight controls against 125 on web. More consequential than the count: Android reports emulator-only testing, and Windows Server CI doesn’t prove the actions are discoverable on a Windows client. There’s deliberately no React Native kit. I wouldn’t replace the cooking app’s Expo screens just to use the action model, or promise five-client chat parity from a web demo.

**What would make me switch.** I’d have two teams ship one workbench handoff with their existing controls: an agent requests review of commit A; only a reviewer may accept it. Change the commit to B while the reviewer is reading. I want to see the agent refused if it tries to approve, the stale approval rejected by the **service**, the reviewer’s note preserved, and a keyboard or screen-reader user able to tell exactly which commit still needs review. Then deliberately drift the MCP schema and check that CI catches it. Finally, have the second team upgrade the pinned kit without help from the first. If that takes less maintenance than our handwritten bindings and preserves the human workflow, I’d adopt AX. For HX, I’d additionally want one centrally maintained component package and that same critical flow passing on the actual supported devices with the people who use them.

I read the repository and guides; I didn’t run the kit. One reason I’d take the pilot seriously is that Ouro documents its own limit: its X-ray guide reports a conformant build that still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. That’s the right distinction. A green check can establish that an interface kept a particular promise; it can’t establish that a reviewer understood what they approved.
